title: Czech — Block 1
subtitle: 30 days to a working foundation
method: **Frequency first.** The 100 commonest Czech words are about half of everything anyone says to you. The first 1,000 get you to roughly 80%. You learn them in that order, not in textbook order — which is why 'beer' arrives before 'library'.

**Chunks before grammar.** You'll learn *Dám si kávu* as one block on day 11 and only later find out it's the accusative case. Grammar here explains patterns you've already used. It never comes first — that's the thing that makes people quit Czech in month two.

**Out loud, every time.** Czech spelling is genuinely one-to-one with sound, so reading aloud IS pronunciation practice — no guessing, no exceptions to memorise. Silent study builds a vocabulary you can recognise but can't speak.
**Spaced repetition, built in.** Each lesson brings back day-1-ago, day-3-ago and day-7-ago words. That schedule is doing most of the actual work; the new words are the easy part.

**What we deliberately skip.** Czech has 7 cases × 3 genders × singular/plural. That's the wall everyone hits. For 30 days you get two cases and one tense, and you'll be able to hold a real exchange. The full tables can wait until you need them.

sounds.ex: DO-brý den · NA shledanou — never moves, no exceptions

sounds.c: á é í ó ú ů ý
sounds.s: same vowel, held twice as long
sounds.ex: This is length, NOT stress. dráha ≠ draha

sounds.s: r and ž at the same time
sounds.ex: Dvořák. Nobody gets it in week one. 'rzh' is close enough to be understood.

sounds.s: ye — softens the letter before it

sounds.ex: led (ice) sounds like 'let' · muž sounds like 'mush'

lessons.title: The stress rule and hello
lessons.why: One rule fixes your accent more than anything else you'll learn: the stress never moves. Get that today and every word after is easier.

grammar.p: Stress is always on syllable one
grammar.d: Whatever the word, however long, the beat lands on the first syllable. Long vowel marks (á, í) mean hold it longer — they do NOT mean stress it. English speakers get this wrong constantly and it's the single biggest giveaway.

drill: Say dobrý den ten times, hammering the DO
Say ahoj to yourself walking around today
Say na shledanou — 'skhle' is one blur, don't hunt for the h

lessons.title: The háček letters
lessons.why: č š ž appear in a huge share of common words. An hour with them today saves you months of mispronouncing everything.

words.e: please / you're welcome / here you go

grammar.p: č = ch, š = sh, ž = zh
grammar.d: The háček (ˇ) turns a plain consonant into its 'sh-family' version. It's completely regular. Once you know the three, you can pronounce any Czech word you see.

drill: Say děkuju until the 'dye' is one sound, not d+y
Prosím does four jobs — please, you're welcome, here you are, and 'pardon?'. Use it for all of them.
Say dobře — that ř will be rough. 'DO-brzheh' is fine for now.

lessons.title: Fifteen words that get you through a day
lessons.why: You now have enough sound rules. Today is pure survival vocabulary — the phrases that let you be a polite human in Czech before you know any grammar at all.

grammar.d: There are no articles at all. 'Kde je záchod' is literally 'where is toilet'. This is one of the genuinely easy things about Czech — stop translating 'the' and you'll sound more natural immediately.
ex: Kde je pivo? = Where's the beer?
Mám auto. = I have a car.

drill: Say all five aloud twice
Nerozumím is your most useful sentence for the next month — make it automatic
Ask yourself Jak se máš? and answer Mám se dobře

lessons.title: To be, and your name
lessons.why: být (to be) is the most common verb in the language and it's irregular, so it gets learned as raw vocabulary now rather than derived later.

grammar.d: The verb ending already tells you who's doing it, so já (I) and ty (you) get left out unless you're emphasising. 'Jsem Christian' — not 'Já jsem Christian'. Saying já every time is a dead giveaway you're translating from English.
ex: Jsem z Austrálie. = I'm from Australia.

drill: Jmenuju se Christian. Těší mě.
Say the full introduction as one flowing line
Review: yesterday's five

lessons.title: Guessing gender from the last letter
lessons.why: Every Czech noun has a gender and it drives everything downstream. There's a rule of thumb that's right about 80% of the time — that's more than enough to start.

grammar.p: Last letter → gender, 80% of the time
grammar.d: Ends in a consonant → masculine. Ends in -a → feminine. Ends in -o → neuter. Chleba is the famous exception (looks feminine, is masculine). Don't memorise exceptions yet — take the 80% and move.

drill: Guess the gender of: stůl, láska, okno
Say each of today's words with its gender out loud
Review: day 4

lessons.title: To have, and one to five
lessons.why: mít is the second workhorse verb, and numbers are the thing you'll need on your very first day in a shop.

grammar.d: A big family of verbs works exactly like mít: -ám for I, -áš for you, -á for he/she. Learn the shape once and it unlocks hundreds of verbs. dělat (to do) → dělám, děláš, dělá.
ex: Mám kávu. = I have a coffee.
Máš auto? = Do you have a car?

drill: Count to five out loud, five times
Mám hodně práce. (I have a lot of work.)
Review: day 5 nouns + their genders

lessons.title: Six to ten, and what it costs
lessons.why: Numbers plus one question gets you through every transaction in the country.

grammar.d: One word covers both. Kolik to stojí? is the single most useful question you'll learn this week — it works for anything you can point at.
ex: Kolik je hodin? = What time is it? (lit. how many hours)

drill: Count 1–10 without pausing
Kolik to stojí? — say it fast, like you actually mean it
Review: day 6 + day 4

lessons.title: The question words
lessons.why: Six words that turn you from someone who answers into someone who can ask. This is where you start having conversations instead of surviving them.

grammar.d: English needs a helper verb — 'do you have'. Czech just uses the statement with a rising tone, or a question word at the front. Máš auto? is both 'you have a car' and 'do you have a car', decided by your voice.
ex: Co to je? = What is that?
Kde je káva? = Where's the coffee?

drill: Ask five questions about things in the room
Co to je? — point at things and say it
Review: day 7 numbers

lessons.title: Saying no to anything
lessons.why: Negation in Czech is one letter. This is the highest-value five minutes in the whole block.

grammar.p: Stick ne- on the front. Done.
grammar.d: Every verb, no exceptions, no auxiliary. mám → nemám. vím → nevím. And unlike English, Czech doubles up happily: Nikdy nic nevím — 'I never don't know nothing' — is correct.

drill: Negate every verb you know so far
Mluvím trochu česky. — you'll use this constantly
Review: day 8 question words

lessons.title: Checkpoint one
lessons.why: No new words. Ten days in, this is where you find out what actually stuck — and what needs another pass.

grammar.d: Cover the English and say each in Czech. Anything you hesitate on for more than two seconds goes on a re-do list for tomorrow.
ex: Hello (formal) / thank you / I don't understand
Do you speak English? / How much is it? / Where's the toilet?
I have / I don't have / I don't know

drill: Introduce yourself out loud: greeting, name, where you're from, nice to meet you
Order a coffee using only what you know
Anything you missed — write it down and re-drill it tomorrow

lessons.title: Dám si kávu — the -u trick
lessons.why: The single most useful pattern in the language for a beginner. One vowel change and you can order anything in the country.

grammar.d: When a feminine noun is the thing being acted on, its final -a flips to -u. káva → kávu. voda → vodu. Neuter (pivo) and masculine inanimate (čaj) don't change at all. That's the accusative case — but you don't need the name, you need the flip.
ex: Mám kávu. = I have a coffee.
Dám si vodu. = I'll have a water.
Dám si pivo. — no change, it's neuter

drill: Order all four out loud
Take every feminine noun you know and flip the -a to -u
Review: day 10 misses

lessons.title: Food worth ordering
lessons.why: Vocabulary you'll use the same week you learn it, all running through yesterday's -u pattern.

grammar.d: Every feminine noun today ends in -a and flips to -u when it's what you want. Neuter and masculine sit still. You now have a rule you can apply to words you've never seen.

drill: Order a full meal out loud
Ještě jedno pivo, prosím — the most Czech sentence there is
Review: day 11

lessons.title: Talking about languages
lessons.why: The conversation you'll have most often as a foreigner, so it's worth being smooth at it.

grammar.d: The second big verb family. mluvit → mluvím, mluvíš, mluví. Compare day 6's mít → mám, máš, má. Two patterns cover most Czech verbs; you now have both.

drill: Mluvím trochu česky, ale učím se. (…but I'm learning.)
Ask three people the question form
Review: day 12

lessons.title: How well, how much
lessons.why: Adverbs let you upgrade every sentence you already own without learning any new grammar.

grammar.d: Nouns decline, verbs conjugate, adjectives agree — adverbs do nothing at all. They're free. Most end in -e or -ě and drop straight in after the verb.

drill: Mluvte pomalu, prosím — you will need this in week one
Add moc or trochu to five sentences you already know
Review: day 13

lessons.title: Wanting things politely
lessons.why: Chci is blunt to the point of rude. Chtěl bych is what an adult actually says.

grammar.d: Chtěl bych if you're male, chtěla bych if you're female. This gender agreement shows up on every past-tense verb too, so meeting it now makes day 23 painless. You say chtěl.
ex: Můžu platit kartou? = Can I pay by card?

drill: Chtěl bych — say it until the khty is one sound
Ask for three things politely
Review: day 14

lessons.title: Where things are
lessons.why: Kde je + a noun answers most of the practical questions you'll have in a strange city.

grammar.d: After kde je the noun stays in its dictionary form — no flip. The -u change from day 11 only applies to the thing being acted on, not the thing being located.

drill: Ask where each of today's places is
Point and say tady / tam
Review: day 15

lessons.title: In Prague — the second case
lessons.why: After v (in) and na (on/at), nouns change again. It's the case you'll read on every sign and hear in every direction.

grammar.d: Praha → v Praze. práce → v práci. The ending shifts, and the pattern is messier than day 11's — for now, learn the handful of places you actually talk about as fixed phrases. doma is a freebie: it's an adverb, it never changes.

drill: Bydlím v Brisbane. Jsem z Austrálie.
Answer Kde bydlíš? out loud
Review: day 16

lessons.title: Checkpoint two
lessons.why: Two cases and two verb patterns in. Time to find the holes before they calcify.

grammar.d: Say each aloud without looking. Two seconds of hesitation means it isn't learned yet.
ex: I'll have a coffee / a water / a beer
I speak a little Czech, but I'm learning
Where do you live? — and answer it
I'd like… / Can I…? / I need…

drill: Order a full meal, start to bill, out loud
Introduce yourself and say where you live and where you're from
Re-drill anything that stalled

lessons.title: The doing verb
lessons.why: dělat is the -ám pattern's poster child and appears in more everyday questions than almost any other verb.

grammar.d: Czech has no separate continuous form. Dělám is both 'I do' and 'I am doing' — context decides. That's one whole English tense you never have to build.

drill: Co děláš? — answer it three different ways
Učím se česky — say it with some conviction
Review: day 18 misses

lessons.title: Knowing and seeing
lessons.why: More -ím family verbs, and the difference between two kinds of 'know' that trips up English speakers.

grammar.d: vím is for facts and information — Vím, kde to je. znám is for being acquainted with a person or place — Znám Prahu. Get these the wrong way round and you'll be understood, but it marks you as a learner.
ex: Myslím, že ano. = I think so.

drill: Nevím vs Neznám — say when each applies
Myslím, že… + finish it three ways
Review: day 19

lessons.title: Coming and going
lessons.why: Movement verbs are irregular and constant. Learning them as fixed phrases beats trying to derive them.

grammar.d: kde = where something IS. kam = where something is GOING. English uses 'where' for both; Czech insists on the difference, and using kde for motion sounds distinctly wrong.
ex: Kam jdeš? = Where are you going?

drill: Kam jdeš? — answer with three destinations
Walking vs driving: jdu vs jedu
Review: day 20

lessons.title: Today, tomorrow, yesterday
lessons.why: Time words are the scaffolding you hang tenses on, and you need them before tomorrow's past tense.

grammar.d: Czech cases mark who does what to whom, so word order is free for emphasis rather than grammar. Dnes pracuju and Pracuju dnes are both correct — the first stresses today, the second stresses working. Whatever comes last tends to carry the weight.

drill: Put dnes, zítra and včera into sentences you know
Nikdy nevím — note the double negative is correct
Review: day 21

lessons.title: What you did — and gender again
lessons.why: The past tense is far easier than English's. One participle plus the verb you learned on day 4.

grammar.p: -l + jsem, and it agrees with you
grammar.d: Take the verb, add -l (male) or -la (female), then bolt on jsem or jsi. That's the whole past tense. The catch from day 15 returns: the ending matches the speaker's gender. You say byl jsem. Third person drops the auxiliary entirely — byl = 'he was'.
ex: Byl jsem doma. = I was at home.
Byl v práci. = He was at work.

drill: Say what you did yesterday, three sentences
Byl jsem — not byla, that's the female form
Review: day 22

lessons.title: Yesterday, out loud
lessons.why: One grammar point only becomes yours when you've used it for something real. Today you narrate your actual day.

grammar.d: Most verbs just take -l on the stem. A few change shape — jít (to go) becomes šel, not 'jdl'. There are maybe a dozen of these worth knowing and they're all extremely common, so they'll stick through use rather than study.

drill: Narrate yesterday in five past-tense sentences, aloud
Note jsem usually sits second in the sentence
Review: day 23

lessons.title: Checkpoint three
lessons.why: Two cases, two verb patterns, present and past. This is a genuine foundation — time to prove it.

grammar.d: All aloud, no looking. Anything that stalls goes on tomorrow's list.
ex: What are you doing? — and three answers
Where were you yesterday? — and answer it
I went / I ate / I drank / I saw
Where are you going? vs Where are you?

drill: Tell the story of yesterday, out loud, one minute
Order a meal, ask the price, ask for the bill
Re-drill the stalls

lessons.title: More than one
lessons.why: Plurals in Czech are a swamp. Here's the shallow end — enough to be understood without drowning in tables.

grammar.d: This is genuinely odd and worth knowing: after 2, 3, 4 the noun takes a normal plural (dvě piva). After 5 and up it switches to the genitive plural, which often looks like the bare stem (pět piv). Nobody will misunderstand you if you get it wrong — but getting it right sounds notably fluent.
ex: dvě piva, tři piva, čtyři piva
pět piv, šest piv, deset piv

drill: Order 2, 3, 4 and then 5 beers
dvě kávy vs pět káv
Review: day 25 misses

lessons.title: Describing things
lessons.why: Adjectives agree with their noun's gender. Three endings and your sentences stop sounding like a telegram.

grammar.d: Masculine takes -ý, feminine -á, neuter -é. dobrý chleba, dobrá káva, dobré pivo. Day 5's last-letter rule is what tells you which to use — the two rules work together.

drill: Describe five things around you
Take every noun you know and attach dobrý in the right form
Review: day 26

lessons.title: Joining sentences up
lessons.why: Connectors are what turn a list of phrases into speech that sounds like a person talking.

grammar.d: Before že and protože there's always a comma — Myslím, že ano. English drops it; Czech never does. Small thing, but it's the kind of detail that makes written Czech look right.
ex: Mluvím trochu česky, ale učím se.

drill: Join five short sentences into longer ones
Mluvím trochu česky, ale učím se — your set-piece line
Review: day 27

lessons.title: The two-minute conversation
lessons.why: Everything from 28 days, assembled into the exchange you'll actually have when someone realises you speak some Czech.

grammar.d: Every piece today is built from grammar you already have. That's the point: you're not learning more, you're proving what you've got is usable.
ex: Jsem z Austrálie. Mluvím trochu česky, ale ještě se učím.

drill: Run the whole conversation out loud, both sides
Record yourself once — you'll want this for day 30 and it's content
Review: day 28

lessons.title: Block one test
lessons.why: Thirty days. Find out honestly what you own, and decide what block two should fix.

grammar.d: Not flashcards — production. Speak for two minutes about yourself with nothing in front of you, then compare against your day 29 recording. If you can do it with hesitation but no English, block one worked.
ex: Order a meal from greeting to bill
Say what you did yesterday and what you're doing tomorrow
Explain that you're learning and ask them to speak slowly

drill: Two minutes, out loud, no notes
List the ten words you still can't retrieve — those seed block two
Tell me how it went and I'll build block two around the gaps

next: Block 2 (days 31–60) opens up the past-vs-future aspect pairs, the genitive, and enough connected listening to follow a real conversation. It gets built from whatever you're still missing on day 30 — so the block-one test matters.
